reply: Slowly it is, and we'll build the tree idea before touching the numbers. Here is the problem: {stem} A probability tree draws an experiment in stages. From the starting point, branches fan out for the first stage; from the end of each branch, more branches fan out for the next stage; and a complete path runs from the start to one of the tips. Every complete path is one way the whole experiment can turn out. A path probability is the product of its conditional branch probabilities, so to find the chance of one path you multiply along that path. When every branch at a stage is equally likely, every complete path gets the same product, so the paths are equally likely and you can simply count them. That is the situation here: the problem tells you how many equally likely paths there are, and how many of them are favorable. Put the favorable count over the total count and give it a try.

reply: That topic isn't open from here, so let's make trees worth the time, because they are the tool that later topics are built on. The multiplication rule and probability trees come down to one statement: a path probability is the product of its conditional branch probabilities. Picture the tree again. Each branch carries the probability of that step happening given everything before it on the path; multiplying those branch probabilities from the start to a tip gives the probability of that complete path, and only that path. Different paths are different outcomes, so their probabilities are never multiplied together. When the branches at each stage are equally likely, every complete path ends up with the same product, which is why the paths in your problem are equally likely and why counting favorable paths against all paths gives the probability. Hold onto two habits: multiply along a path, never across paths, and count each complete path exactly once. With those in place, the spinner problem is a short count, and we'll return to it next.
